idiom_name: HashMap<K, Supplier<V>> plus a static factory(Consumer<Builder>) configuration method
implementation_notes: This is the catalog's own reference realization: the separated Builder and Factory interfaces collapse into java.util.function.Consumer (the configuration callback) and Supplier (the builder), the kit being a static method that fills a HashMap and returns name -> map.get(name).get(), with method references such as Sword::new as the builders, so no concrete factory classes are written. What replaces the classic structure: the map plus those two java.util.function types; an abstract factory hierarchy is only justified when products arrive in families that must stay consistent. Neighbouring library mechanism: java.util.ServiceLoader performs the same dispatch over implementations discovered from the classpath (META-INF/services files or a module's provides clause), so prefer it over a hand-rolled registry when discovery without recompilation, not in-code configuration, is the point.
pitfalls: Map.get returns null for an unregistered key, so the classic failure is a NullPointerException inside the lambda rather than a named error - check and throw an exception that lists the known keys.
A HashMap published to several threads must be filled before it is shared; later mutation needs ConcurrentHashMap or an immutable snapshot (Map.copyOf).
ServiceLoader providers need a public no-argument constructor (or a static provider() method) plus the module's uses/provides wiring; a missing provider is silently absent rather than an error.
